claim: Genes upregulated in the forebrain involved in cell-cell communication include Dkk1, Scube1, Scube2, and Wnt8b.
source: In addition, several genes involved in cell-cell communication were upregulated in a region-specific fashion, including Dkk1, Scube1, Scube2, and Wnt8b in the forebrain, Cldn10, Fgf17, and Spry1 in the midbrain/r1 region, and Fgf3, Plxna2, Robo2, and Sema4f in the hindbrain.
evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes upregulated in the midbrain/r1 region involved in cell-cell communication include Cldn10, Fgf17, and Spry1.
source: In addition, several genes involved in cell-cell communication were upregulated in a region-specific fashion, including Dkk1, Scube1, Scube2, and Wnt8b in the forebrain, Cldn10, Fgf17, and Spry1 in the midbrain/r1 region, and Fgf3, Plxna2, Robo2, and Sema4f in the hindbrain.
evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes upregulated in the hindbrain involved in cell-cell communication include Fgf3, Plxna2, Robo2, and Sema4f.
source: In addition, several genes involved in cell-cell communication were upregulated in a region-specific fashion, including Dkk1, Scube1, Scube2, and Wnt8b in the forebrain, Cldn10, Fgf17, and Spry1 in the midbrain/r1 region, and Fgf3, Plxna2, Robo2, and Sema4f in the hindbrain.
evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression analysis.

claim: The results are consistent with the emergence of region-specific cell identities along the anterior-posterior axis of the E7.5-E9.0 cranial neural plate.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cranial neural plate cells from E8.5 and E8.75–9.0 embryos were pooled for spatial analysis.
source: To characterize the spatial organization of transcription in the cranial neural plate, we pooled cranial neural plate cells from E8.5 (7–9 somites) and E8.75–9.0 (10+somites) embryos, when strong regional patterns of gene expression were apparent, and we reapplied diffusion component analysis on the aggregated data (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the approach for spatial analysis.

claim: The top diffusion component (DC0) in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset reproduced the anterior-posterior order of known markers of the forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain regions.
source: The top diffusion component in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset (DC0) reproduced the anterior-posterior order of known markers of the forebrain (Six3, Otx1, Otx2), midbrain/r1 (En1, Wnt1), and hindbrain (Gbx2) regions, indicating that this diffusion component correctly orders cells relative to the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffusion component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: DC0 correctly orders cells relative to the anterior-posterior axis.
source: The top diffusion component in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset (DC0) reproduced the anterior-posterior order of known markers of the forebrain (Six3, Otx1, Otx2), midbrain/r1 (En1, Wnt1), and hindbrain (Gbx2) regions, indicating that this diffusion component correctly orders cells relative to the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between DC0 and known markers.

claim: DC0 recapitulated the anterior-posterior order of markers of more refined transcriptional domains, such as the future telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain-hindbrain boundary, and rhombomeres 2–5.
source: In addition, DC0 recapitulated the anterior-posterior order of markers of more refined transcriptional domains, such as the future telencephalon (Foxg1, Lhx2), diencephalon (Barhl2), midbrain-hindbrain boundary (Fgf8), and rhombomeres 2–5 (Hoxb1, Hoxb2, Egr2; Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffusion component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The second diffusion component (DC1) in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset displayed a strong anterior-posterior signature.
source: The second diffusion component in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset (DC1) also displayed a strong anterior-posterior signature, with DC1 separating genes expressed in the midbrain/r1 domain from genes expressed in the forebrain and hindbrain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffusion component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: DC1 separates genes expressed in the midbrain/r1 domain from genes expressed in the forebrain and hindbrain.
source: The second diffusion component in the pooled E8.5–9.0 dataset (DC1) also displayed a strong anterior-posterior signature, with DC1 separating genes expressed in the midbrain/r1 domain from genes expressed in the forebrain and hindbrain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffusion component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: DC0 and DC1 correlate with anterior-posterior pattern, with DC0 ordering cells along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: These results indicate that DC0 and DC1 correlate with anterior-posterior pattern, with DC0 ordering cells along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diffusion component analysis.

claim: 483 genes in 11 clusters are predicted to be patterned relative to the anterior-posterior axis of the cranial neural plate.
source: This analysis identified 483 genes in 11 clusters that are predicted to be patterned relative to the anterior-posterior axis of the cranial neural plate (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spatial analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The 11 anterior-posterior clusters were assigned to the future forebrain (clusters 0 and 7), midbrain/r1 (clusters 3 and 5), and hindbrain (clusters 4, 6, and 10), with some clusters spanning multiple domains (clusters 1, 2, 8, and 9).
source: By comparing with markers for specific anterior-posterior domains (Figure 3C), we assigned these clusters to the future forebrain (clusters 0 and 7), midbrain/r1 (clusters 3 and 5), and hindbrain (clusters 4, 6, and 10), with some clusters spanning multiple domains (clusters 1, 2, 8, and 9; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a classification based on comparison with known markers, with reference to figures.

claim: The midbrain and rhombomere 1 shared clear transcriptional signatures that distinguish them from other regions of the cranial neural plate.
source: We note that although the midbrain and rhombomere 1 shared clear transcriptional signatures that distinguish them from other regions of the cranial neural plate, there were also clear differences between these domains, consistent with their respective midbrain and hindbrain identities.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: There were clear differences between the midbrain and rhombomere 1, consistent with their respective midbrain and hindbrain identities.
source: We note that although the midbrain and rhombomere 1 shared clear transcriptional signatures that distinguish them from other regions of the cranial neural plate, there were also clear differences between these domains, consistent with their respective midbrain and hindbrain identities.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Hundreds of genes are expressed in a small number of discrete domains along the anterior-posterior axis, corresponding to the metameric organization of the forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain regions.
source: Together, these results provide a comprehensive description of the modular organization of gene expression in the cranial neural plate and reveal that hundreds of genes are expressed in a small number of discrete domains along the anterior-posterior axis, corresponding to the metameric organization of the forebrain, midbrain/r1, and hindbrain regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial analysis.

claim: Of 483 genes predicted to be patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, 162 had published images of in situ hybridization or protein immuno-staining experiments in the E8.5–9.0 cranial region.
source: Of 483 genes predicted to be patterned along the anterior-posterior axis, 162 had published images of in situ hybridization or protein immuno-staining experiments in the E8.5–9.0 cranial region (Theiler stages 12–14; Theiler, 1989).

claim: 141 of the 162 genes with published data (87%) were expressed in region-specific domains along the anterior-posterior axis that were consistent with the patterns predicted by the analysis.
source: We found that 141 of the 162 genes for which data were available (87%) were expressed in region-specific domains along the anterior-posterior axis that were consistent with the patterns predicted by our analysis (Supplementary file 7, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing predictions to published data.

claim: The remaining 21 genes were expressed in the predicted domain(s) in addition to one or more regions not predicted by the analysis, likely due to the increased sensitivity of in situ hybridization compared with scRNA-seq.
source: The remaining 21 genes were expressed in the predicted domain(s) in addition to one or more regions not predicted by our analysis, likely due to the increased sensitivity of in situ hybridization compared with scRNA-seq (Lohoff et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the validation results, supported by a citation.

claim: Ordering gene expression relative to DC0 recapitulated the expression patterns of 141 known genes and predicted patterned expression along the anterior-posterior axis for an additional 321 genes whose expression in the developing cranial neural plate has not previously been analyzed.

evidence: This is a summary of the validation and prediction results.

claim: 123 genes encoding transcription factors are predicted to be spatially regulated along the anterior-posterior axis of the E8.5–9.0 cranial neural plate.
source: This approach identified 123 genes encoding transcription factors that are predicted to be spatially regulated along the anterior-posterior axis of the E8.5–9.0 cranial neural plate (54 shown in Figure 3E–G; see Supplementary file 8 for full list).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing spatially patterned genes with transcription factor databases.

claim: Otx2 is a homeodomain transcription factor that is required to form the forebrain and midbrain.
source: These include Otx2, a homeodomain transcription factor that is required to form the forebrain and midbrain (Acampora et al., 1995; Matsuo et al., 1995; Ang et al., 1996), as well as genes required for specific aspects of development in the forebrain (Foxg1, Hesx1, Rax, Six3; Xuan et al., 1995; Mathers et al., 1997; Dattani et al., 1998; Lagutin et al., 2003), midbrain, or rhombomere 1 (En1, En2, Fgf8, Gbx2, Pax2, Pax5; Joyner et al., 1991; Wurst et al., 1994; Crossley et al., 1996; Favor et al., 1996; Torres et al., 1996; Wassarman et al., 1997; Millet et al., 1999; Schwarz et al., 1999; Liu and Joyner, 2001b; Li et al., 2002; Chi et al., 2003),

source: These include Otx2, a homeodomain transcription factor that is required to form the forebrain and midbrain (Acampora et al., 1995; Matsuo et al., 1995; Ang et al., 1996), as well as genes required for specific aspects of development in the forebrain (Foxg1, Hesx1, Rax, Six3; Xuan et al., 1995; Mathers et al., 1997; Dattani et al., 1998; Lagutin et al., 2003), midbrain, or rhombomere 1 (En1, En2, Fgf8, Gbx2, Pax2, Pax5; Joyner et al., 1991; Wurst et al., 1994; Crossley et al., 1996; Favor et al., 1996; Torres et al., 1996; Wassarman et al., 1997; Millet et al., 1999; Schwarz et al., 1999; Liu and Joyner, 2001b; Li et al., 2002; Chi et al., 2003),

source: These include Otx2, a homeodomain transcription factor that is required to form the forebrain and midbrain (Acampora et al., 1995; Matsuo et al., 1995; Ang et al., 1996), as well as genes required for specific aspects of development in the forebrain (Foxg1, Hesx1, Rax, Six3; Xuan et al., 1995; Mathers et al., 1997; Dattani et al., 1998; Lagutin et al., 2003), midbrain, or rhombomere 1 (En1, En2, Fgf8, Gbx2, Pax2, Pax5; Joyner et al., 1991; Wurst et al., 1994; Crossley et al., 1996; Favor et al., 1996; Torres et al., 1996; Wassarman et al., 1997; Millet et al., 1999; Schwarz et al., 1999; Liu and Joyner, 2001b; Li et al., 2002; Chi et al., 2003),
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: In addition to patterning along the anterior-posterior axis, cell fate determination along the mediolateral axis of the cranial neural plate is essential for neural tube closure, neuronal differentiation, and neural circuit formation (Shimamura et al., 1997; Agarwala et al., 2001; Hoch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spatially regulated gene expression along the dorsal-ventral axis has been systematically characterized in the developing spinal cord.
source: However, although spatially regulated gene expression along the dorsal-ventral axis has been systematically characterized in the developing spinal cord (Delile et al., 2019; Sampath Kumar et al., 2023), the transcriptional cascades that govern mediolateral patterning in the cranial neural plate are not well understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The transcriptional cascades that govern mediolateral patterning in the cranial neural plate are not well understood.
source: However, although spatially regulated gene expression along the dorsal-ventral axis has been systematically characterized in the developing spinal cord (Delile et al., 2019; Sampath Kumar et al., 2023), the transcriptional cascades that govern mediolateral patterning in the cranial neural plate are not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: DC2 was positively correlated with laterally expressed genes (Pax3, Pax7, Tfap2a, Zic1) and negatively correlated with markers of the ventral midline (Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Ptch1, Shh).
source: In contrast to DC0 and DC1, which correlate with markers of anterior-posterior pattern, DC2 was positively correlated with laterally expressed genes (Pax3, Pax7, Tfap2a, Zic1) and negatively correlated with markers of the ventral midline (floor plate; Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Ptch1, Shh; Figure 4A–C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffusion component analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: DC2 can be used to order genes with respect to the mediolateral axis.
source: These results indicate that DC2 can be used to order genes with respect to the mediolateral axis.

source: This analysis identified 253 genes in 7 clusters that display high information content along DC2 and are predicted to be mediolaterally patterned (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, Supplementary file 6).

claim: Two clusters (1 and 2) are predicted to have increased expression in lateral domains.
source: These include four clusters (0, 4, 5, and 6) predicted to have increased expression in the midline and two clusters (1 and 2) predicted to have increased expression in lateral domains.
evidence: This is a classification based on the spatial analysis.

claim: Genes predicted to be expressed in medial clusters include effectors of SHH signaling (Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Nkx2-2, and Nkx2-9).
source: Genes predicted to be expressed in medial clusters include effectors of SHH signaling (Foxa2, Nkx6-1, Nkx2-2, and Nkx2-9; Sasaki et al., 1997; Briscoe et al., 1999; Sander et al., 2000; Dessaud et al., 2008; Ribes and Briscoe, 2009; Nishi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis, supported by citations to prior literature.

source: In addition, genes predicted to be expressed in lateral clusters include factors that have been shown to promote dorsal cell fates (Msx1, Msx2; Bach et al., 2003), suppress neuronal differentiation (Hes1, Hes3; Hirata et al., 2001; Hatakeyama et al., 2004), and regulate cranial neural tube closure (Gli3, Sp8, Zic2, Zic5; Nagai et al., 2000; Bell et al., 2003; Treichel et al., 2003; Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A subset of genes was expressed in continuously increasing or decreasing patterns relative to DC2, reminiscent of gradients.
source: A subset of genes was expressed in continuously increasing or decreasing patterns relative to DC2, reminiscent of gradients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).

claim: Nearly two-thirds of genes that were clustered relative to DC2 were also patterned along the orthogonal axis.
source: Nearly one-third of genes that were clustered relative to DC0, and nearly two-thirds of genes that were clustered relative to DC2, were also patterned along the orthogonal axis (Supplementary file 6), suggesting a high degree of overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the spatial clustering results.

claim: There is a high degree of overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning systems.

claim: 870 genes with high mutual information content with respect to anterior-posterior and mediolaterally correlated diffusion components were identified.

source: Moreover, because we used the full diffusion space, the resulting clusters integrate more than one cartesian axis at once and capture more fine-grained spatial patterns.

claim: The multiscale analysis includes genes identified from analysis of DC0 and DC2, as well as additional genes not identified from analysis of a single diffusion component.
source: These include the genes identified in our analyses of DC0 (anterior-posterior pattern in Figure 3) and DC2 (mediolateral pattern in Figure 4), as well as additional genes that were not identified from analysis of a single diffusion component (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 6), suggesting that these expression patterns reflect inputs from a combination of anterior-posterior and mediolateral spatial cues.

claim: The expression patterns of genes identified in the multiscale analysis reflect inputs from a combination of anterior-posterior and mediolateral spatial cues.
source: These include the genes identified in our analyses of DC0 (anterior-posterior pattern in Figure 3) and DC2 (mediolateral pattern in Figure 4), as well as additional genes that were not identified from analysis of a single diffusion component (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 6), suggesting that these expression patterns reflect inputs from a combination of anterior-posterior and mediolateral spatial cues.

source: In addition, this distance cutoff assigned midline transcripts in the midbrain/r1 region (Foxa1, Foxa2) to a different cluster from midline transcripts in the forebrain (Gsc, Nkx2-1, Nkx2-4), and separately clustered lateral transcripts in the midbrain/r1 region (Pax5, Pax8) from lateral transcripts that were more broadly expressed along the anterior-posterior axis (Msx1, Msx2, Pax7, Zic1, Zic5; Figure 5D, Supplementary file 6).

claim: At D=6, lateral transcripts in the midbrain/r1 region were separately clustered from lateral transcripts that were more broadly expressed along the anterior-posterior axis.

evidence: This describes the clustering at intermediate stringency, with reference to figures.

source: Notably, the majority of these genes were predicted to be patterned along both mediolateral and anterior-posterior axes, suggesting that neural precursor transcripts arrayed along a one-dimensional axis in the developing spinal cord are often patterned in two dimensions in the cranial neural plate.
